messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 63
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Construction Worker
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
- Pcl5: 68

He arrives a few minutes early for every session, always in the same faded denim jacket, the sleeves frayed at the cuffs. He sits on the edge of the chair, hands resting on his knees, fingers drumming a slow, steady rhythm. He tells me his name is Tane. He is sixty-three, a widower, and still works construction—“just the small jobs now,” he says, “nothing too high.”

Tane was born in a small village in the islands, the eldest of five children. He came to the mainland in his twenties to find work, and for a long time he sent money home. He met Ana here, at a church picnic. She was kind, he remembers, with a laugh that made people turn their heads. They married quickly. Within a year, the first slap came—a sudden, shocking thing, followed by her tears, her apologies, her promise it would never happen again. And it didn’t, for a while. Then it did.

He describes the pattern as if reciting a weather forecast: the slow build of tension, her sharp words, then the explosion—a shove, a punch, a yank of his hair. He learned to read the signs. He would make himself small, stay quiet, move slowly around the house. “I’m a big man,” he says, looking down at his calloused hands. “I could have stopped her with one hand. But I loved her. And I was ashamed.”

The worst night came when he was fifty-eight. She had been drinking. He had come home late from a job, tired, his back aching. She accused him of seeing someone else. He tried to walk away, but she followed him into the bedroom. He remembers the lamp hitting his temple, the glass shattering. He remembers her on top of him, her fists landing on his chest, his face. He did not fight back. “I just lay there,” he says. “I thought, if she kills me, at least it will be over.”

She died six months later—a heart attack, sudden, at the grocery store. The police came to his door. He was a widower. People told him how sorry they were. He said nothing.

Now, three years later, Tane cannot stop checking the locks. He does it three times before bed, sometimes four. He avoids crowded places, especially churches. When a coworker raises a voice on the job site—yelling for a tool, a warning to step back—Tane flinches. His hands shake. He has to walk away, find a corner, and breathe. His foreman has noticed. They moved him to ground-level work, sorting materials, because he froze on a scaffolding last spring, gripping the rail, unable to move. “I don’t tell them the truth,” he says. “I say it’s my back.”

At night he lies awake, or he dreams of her. Not the good dreams—the dreams where she is alive again, standing over him, her hand raised. He wakes up sweating, his chest tight, a scream caught in his throat. His daughter calls from the islands every Sunday. He tells her he is fine. He has not told anyone about the beatings. Not once, not ever. “What would they think of me?” he asks. “A man who let his wife hurt him.”

He works because he must—there is no pension, no savings. But the work is becoming harder. The noise of the jackhammer makes his heart pound. The shadow of a crane overhead sends a cold wave through him. He has started drinking after shifts, just a beer or two, to quiet the jumpy feeling inside. He knows it is not helping. He knows he cannot keep this up.

He looks at me across the room, his fingers finally still. “I don’t want to be angry,” he says. “But I am. At her. At myself. At God for letting her die before I could fix it.” He pauses. “I don’t know how to stop being angry.”
